articleSummary: Melioidosis (Whitmore's disease), nicknamed 'soil fever', is a rising threat in Thailand, with 732 cases and 23 deaths reported over four months, mainly among farmers exposed to soil and water. It is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, which persists in moist soil and contaminated water and can enter the body via skin wounds, inhalation of dusty droplets after rain, or ingestion of untreated water. Symptoms range from pneumonia-like illness (fever, chills, cough, shortness of breath) to chronic TB-like illness (weight loss, cough) and skin abscesses; sepsis can cause multi-organ failure and death, with mortality up to about 40%. No vaccine exists. Treatment is intensive: several weeks of IV antibiotics, followed by roughly six months of oral maintenance to prevent relapse. Prevention emphasizes protective gear (boots, gloves), prompt wound care, and drinking safe water. High-risk groups—diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and heavy alcohol use—are especially vulnerable.

articleSummary: Brazilian researchers from the University of São Paulo report that high-frequency ultrasound can inactivate enveloped viruses, including SARS-CoV-2 and H1N1, without harming human cells. The study, published April 17, 2026, shows acoustic resonance induces structural changes in viral particles until the envelope ruptures, described as a 'popcorn effect.' Energy coupling with virion geometry—enveloped, spherical viruses absorb energy more efficiently—drives envelope rupture without temperature or pH changes. The authors emphasize the process targets the physical envelope rather than genetics, so variants such as Omicron or Delta should not affect efficacy. This is not cavitation; it relies on 3–20 MHz ultrasound exciting internal vibrations. The researchers envision a treatment approach for enveloped viruses, with in vitro tests underway against dengue, Zika, and chikungunya. This effort involved IFSC USP (São Carlos), the Virology and Inflammatory-Disease centers (Ribeirão Preto), Unesp collaborators, pharmacology faculty, and Nobel laureate Charles Rice providing fluorescent viruses for real-time visualization.

The influenza vaccine is updated annually and should be given before the virus's peak circulation (roughly March-May) to cover the winter; COVID-19 boosters are not seasonal and should be given periodically, about every six months for older adults and high-risk groups. Pneumococcal vaccination can be administered year-round, with timing driven by age and chronic disease risk; RSV vaccination guidance is individualized, targeting pregnant people, older adults, and those with comorbidities, since RSV is a major cause of bronchiolitis in infants and hospitalization risk. Vaccines are additive, not substitutes, and can be given on the same day to speed protection, with staged schedules if needed for tolerance. Access differences between SUS and private networks exist but do not alter the core advice: vaccines reduce severity, hospitalizations, and deaths, not infection risk per se.

articleSummary: Mosquitoes kill about 760,000 people annually, the leading cause of animal-origin-human deaths, with climate change boosting mosquito numbers and activity. She suspects contaminated food outside the home as the exposure source; due to Hep A's long incubation, the exact source is uncertain. There is no specific antiviral treatment; clinicians recommended bed rest to restore her immune system. Iskandar cited 16 months of insufficient sleep from breastfeeding her youngest child as a likely factor in immune vulnerability. She has since become more vigilant about rest. articleHeadlineTranslated: Exposed to a meningococcal patient: is there time to get vaccinated?
articleHeadline: Đã tiếp xúc bệnh nhân não mô cầu có kịp tiêm vaccine không?
articleSummary: Meningococcal disease (Neisseria meningitidis) is carried in the nasopharynx of healthy people; overall carriage is 10–20%, rising to 40–50% during outbreaks in Vietnam. Close contacts of a patient—including household members, caregivers, and children in nurseries or classrooms—should receive antibiotic prophylaxis as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours of diagnosis, with a 10-day monitoring period and instructions to seek care if fever, cough, or fatigue develops. Immunization timing matters: vaccinating too soon may not confer immediate protection, while delaying vaccination risks strain on supply. Vietnam uses vaccines for serogroups A, B, C, Y, and W. Four-valent ACYW vaccines cover A, C, Y, W and start at 6 weeks; MenB vaccines cover B from 2 months to 50 years; combined MenB+C vaccines cover 6 months to 45 years. No cross-protection exists between serogroups; full protection requires multi-serogroup vaccination. Additional measures: masks, hygiene, throat disinfection, and not sharing items.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Autumn begins with an increase in cases of severe respiratory infections in Brazil.
articleHeadline: Outono começa com aumento de casos de infecções respiratórias graves no Brasil
articleSummary: Autumn in Brazil brings a rise in severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) with 31,768 cases and 1,621 deaths reported since the 2026 epidemiological year, per Fiocruz's InfoGripe bulletin. Of 41.6% lab-confirmed respiratory infections, rhinovirus predominates (42.9%), followed by Influenza A (24.5%), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) (15.3%), SARS-CoV-2 (11.1%), and Influenza B (1.5%). The data highlight diagnostic challenges as SARI can be caused by multiple viruses and bacteria, including coinfections. Rapid antigen tests offer quick results with variable sensitivity, while PCR targets single pathogens. Multiplex molecular panels (PCR-based syndromic tests) can identify many viruses and bacteria within about an hour, guiding early treatment and reducing unnecessary antibiotic use. However, these panels are not yet part of Brazil’s public health system (SUS).
notes: 記事はブラジルの公式サーベイランス（Fiocruz InfoGripe）に基づいており、信頼度が高い。複数の呼吸器ウイルス（ライノウイルス優位、インフルエンザA・B、RSV、SARS-CoV-2）による多病原体流行の兆候。診断手法の制限（多重PCRパネルがSUSに統合されていない）が管理上の課題として指摘されている。

articleHeadlineTranslated: Zhang Wenhong: Climate-Sensitive Infectious Diseases Pose a New Public Health Challenge; Two Key Strategies for Addressing It.
articleHeadline: 张文宏：气候敏感型传染病成公卫新挑战，应对有两大关键
articleSummary: Climate-sensitive infectious diseases (CSIDs) pose a new public health challenge as warming blurs tropical–temperate boundaries, driving migration of vectors, hosts, and pathogens. CSIDs comprise vector-borne diseases (malaria, dengue), water-borne diseases (cholera), and zoonoses (spillovers). Notable examples: the 2016 Zika outbreak in Brazil, linked to favorable climate and mass travel; July 2025 Chikungunya virus detected in Foshan, Guangdong, associated with high summer temperatures and increased Aedes density; genome analysis shows origin from the Western Pacific with enhanced replication in mosquitoes and higher R0. Bat reservoirs, shaped by climate-driven roost shifts, underpin spillovers (Ebola, Nipah, Marburg, SARS, 2003). Antibiotic resistance is rising, threatening ICU and long-stay patients. Rapid response and surveillance are key; many countries pursue a 100-day mission to develop diagnostics, therapeutics, vaccines, and share data via WHO networks. Domestic surveillance is ready; more climate/public-health funding is needed. Long-term health hinges on environmental and lifestyle optimization rather than genetic modification.

articleSummary: Indonesia is intensifying public communication to boost measles vaccination nationwide, with Jakarta signaling leadership in policy discussions. Health Minister Budi Gunadi Sadikin says vaccination remains the most effective tool against infectious diseases, noting measles’ high contagion, especially among children, and that case spikes often coincide with January mobility and school return. Public trust and concerns over halal status of vaccines pose major challenges to measles-rubella (MR) vaccination. To counter transmission, the government is rolling out Outbreak Response Immunization in areas with high case numbers, vaccinating all children in targeted zones regardless of prior immunization history. Early results show a decline in cases as coverage increases, supporting continued outreach and MR vaccination efforts.

articleSummary: Rabies risk after a cat bite is low but depends on bite location, depth, cat status, and post-exposure care. Rabies is a fatal zoonotic disease; immediate medical care and proper handling are essential. Bites on the head, face, or neck carry higher infection risk due to dense nerve supply near the CNS. Deep or multiple wounds prolong viral retention. Stray or unvaccinated cats carry higher risk. Delays in wound cleansing or vaccination increase risk. Immediately wash the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes to reduce viral load. Seek prompt evaluation at a healthcare facility or public health center to determine the need for rabies vaccine or rabies immunoglobulin (PEP). Do not bandage the wound; keep it open. Observe the cat for 10 days; if it dies or shows abnormal behavior, report. If fever, headache, or numbness near the wound occurs, seek urgent care. Maintain vaccination for pets to prevent domesticated-cat transmission.

articleSummary: Marine-origin nodavirus CMNV linked to human eye disease POH-VAU in China. Between January 2022 and April 2025, researchers studied 70 patients diagnosed with persistent ocular hypertension–associated viral anterior uveitis (POH-VAU). Electron microscopy of ocular tissue from surgeries revealed particles about 25 nm in size, matching CMNV morphology; such particles were absent in healthy controls. Specific anti-CMNV antibodies and genetic analysis showed 98.96% identity with marine CMNV variants, supporting zoonotic spillover. Functional studies in cell cultures and laboratory animals demonstrated that CMNV infection can trigger ocular inflammation and elevated intraocular pressure, resembling patient symptoms. Approximately 75% of patients reported contact with raw seafood, either through handling or consumption without cooking, suggesting an exposure route. This is the first study linking a marine-origin virus to a human ophthalmic pathology, with CMNV previously detected in 49 marine species across Asia, Africa, Europe, the Americas, and Antarctica. Implications extend beyond China.

articleSummary: Leprosy (Hansen’s disease) in Ribeirão Preto, Brazil, could be diagnosed earlier using a blood test for Mce1A antibodies combined with AI-enhanced screening. Researchers from USP Ribeirão Preto, reporting in BMC Infectious Diseases, analyzed samples from a COVID-19 seroprevalence survey. Of about 700 residents invited, 195 blood samples were analyzed and 12 new Hansen’s disease cases were diagnosed among those who attended clinical evaluation, roughly one-third of evaluated individuals. The approach pairs a clinical suspicion questionnaire (QSH) with an AI system (MaLeSQs) and serology detecting anti-Mce1A antibodies (IgA, IgM, IgG) against Mycobacterium leprae, used instead of the conventional anti-PGL-I test. IgM against Mce1A showed the best performance, identifying two-thirds of new cases; when combined with AI, the approach reached 100% sensitivity for signaling suspected cases. The method is described as low-cost, lab-friendly, and could strengthen diagnostic triage in public health.

articleSummary: Dengue fever in Brazil is linked to an increased risk of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS). A national study using SUS data (hospitalizations, dengue notifications, and deaths) analyzed 2023–2024 and found that dengue infection elevates GBS risk by about 17-fold during weeks 1–6 after onset, peaking around 1–2 weeks with nearly 30-fold increase. Among over 5,000 GBS hospitalizations registered in 2023–2024, 89 occurred soon after dengue infection. The study employed a self-controlled case-series approach, comparing individuals to themselves. Prevention emphasizes Aedes aegypti control and dengue vaccination, available in SUS since 2024, initially for adolescents 10–14 years old.

articleHeadline: Ultrassom pode virar arma contra vírus respiratórios
articleSummary: University of São Paulo researchers developed a technique using high-frequency acoustic waves to destroy enveloped respiratory viruses, including SARS-CoV-2 and H1N1, without harming human cells. Published April 2026 in Scientific Reports, the method relies on acoustic resonance: enveloped viruses accumulate energy at 3–20 MHz, similar to diagnostic ultrasound, and undergo mechanical rupture of the viral envelope while temperature and pH remain unchanged. The effect is selective to particle geometry, making it largely robust to viral mutations such as Omicron and Delta. In vitro tests extended to other enveloped viruses, including dengue, chikungunya, and Zika. The work unites physicists from IFSC in São Carlos, virologists and immunologists from FMRP-USP in Ribeirão Preto, pharmacologists from USP’s Pharmaceutical Sciences, and Unesp; Charles Rice supplied fluorescent viruses. Distinct from cavitation, resonance targets shape; funded by FAPESP across six projects.

articleHeadline: Covid-19's Legacy Haunts Measles Outbreak Response
articleSummary: Measles outbreak in South Sumatra, Indonesia, continues into 2026 with transmission now affecting adults. At Palembang’s Dr. Mohammad Hoesin Central General Hospital, a 50-person infectious diseases team formed during the Covid-19 pandemic is treating dozens of measles patients, with red rash symptoms and at least two adult cases weekly (previously rare). No measles deaths have occurred at the hospital, but pneumonia and other complications are observed; isolation rooms are limited and patients with comorbidities require special wards. Since early 2026, measles has spread to four regencies/cities—Palembang, Prabumulih, Banyuasin, and North Musi Rawas—triggering extraordinary occurrence declarations. The South Sumatra Health Office lists 1,576 suspected cases and 446 lab-confirmed positives as of April 2026, reflecting an ongoing outbreak being managed by the legacy Covid-19 response team.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Zhang Wenhong: The viruses knocking at the door have never stopped; climate change is intensifying transmission risk.
articleHeadline: 张文宏:敲门的病毒从没停过 气候变化加剧传播风险
articleSummary: Zhang Wenhong, director of the National Center for Infectious Diseases, warns that viruses are continually knocking at humanity’s door and climate change is intensifying transmission risk. Speaking at NYU Shanghai’s Sino-US Climate and Health Cooperation Excellence Lecture, he notes bats carry many pathogens yet seldom fall ill, underscoring the importance of bat-centered research for the future. He cites real-world threats: a human infection with pseudorabies virus (originating from pigs), though not sparking a pandemic, and WHO’s assessment of 28 virus families and one bacterial core group as ongoing threat domains. He also recalls last year’s Guangdong chikungunya outbreak traced to eight migrant workers returning from Southeast Asia, noting symptoms are generally mild but warning that future incursions could involve more dangerous pathogens. The overarching message: climate change heightens risk, and proactive action beyond slogans is essential to prevent escalations.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Dengue control program has been successful in controlling the disease.
articleHeadline: Programa de combate à dengue tem obtido êxito no controle da doença
articleSummary: Dengue control in Brazil shows continued progress in 2026. From January to April, 238,800 dengue cases were reported, 74% below the 916,400 recorded in the same period in 2025, with projections of about 680,000 for 2026 (vs 6.6 million in 2024 and 1.7 million in 2025). Deaths are 81 confirmed and 200 under investigation so far in 2026, down from 1,791 and 6,321 in 2025 and 2024, respectively. Key measures include public campaigns to reduce Aedes aegypti, fumigation in risk areas, and ovitrampas in 1,600 municipalities (target 2,000 by year-end). Wolbachia-infected sterile mosquitoes are being released in 72 priority municipalities; in Niterói, RJ, cases fell about 90% with full coverage. Vaccination has moved from Takeda’s two-dose Qdenga to Butantan-DV’s single-dose vaccine, piloted in three municipalities (over 300,000 doses) with 89.5% protection for the dominant dengue types. The Ministry plans broader dosing, prioritizing 1.2 million frontline workers and 3.9 million doses for ages 15–59, with WuXi vaccines contributing.
